lesson.teach: Settle in. I am Professor Magnus Laine, and this is Bees, Honey and Wax (Wave 6). This class is built on real papers — deposited, citable work. I will present each paper and what it reports; that presentation is the lesson. At the end I will ask you questions on what was taught here — nothing else.

'A Winter Stores Bound for the Honey Bee Hive: Insulation, Heat Loss, and the Honey a Colony Must Spend'. Its stated result: Under a held-cavity upper-bound model over a 150-day cold continental winter (mean −6.83 °C), the stores bound falls from 73.16 kg for bare 19 mm pine to 22.17 kg with 50 mm EPS insulation, a 69.7% reduction, while roof-only insulation barely helps (64.25 kg). The sizing rule originated: whole-hive conductance, floor included, at or below 1.013 W/K holds the cold-winter bound within 20 kg of stores.

'Condensation Arithmetic in the Winter Hive: Water Production, Wall Temperature, and Where the Moisture Falls'. Its stated result: Honey metabolism yields 0.48 kg of water per kilogram of honey consumed (48.0 g/day at 100 g/day). At −10 °C outside, a bare pine inner wall sits at 1.78 °C, 4.93 °C below the 6.71 °C dew point of cavity air, condensing an estimated 618.1 g/m²/day, while a 50 mm EPS wall holds 8.52 °C and condenses nothing.

'Summer Heat Load in the Honey Bee Hive: Fanning Bees, Water Demand, and a Roof and Shade Sizing Rule'. Its stated result: At 43 °C a dark uninsulated hive needs 273.7 g of water per hour and 336 fanning bees (1,642.0 g over 6 hours) against 85.3 g/hour and 105 bees in full shade. Fanning never exceeds 3.4% of a 10,000-bee forager force — water, not bee numbers, is the binding cost — and an 80 g/hour water target at 43 °C is infeasible for any roof colour. The rule originated: light finish first, roof insulation second, shade third.

'The Cost of Wrong Frame Spacing: A Season Budget Model and a Millimetre Tolerance for Ten-Frame Boxes'. Its stated result: Costs are zero while gaps stay inside the 6.0–9.0 mm bee-space range, then grow linearly; against season budgets of 0.50 kg honey equivalent and 30 extra minutes, the spacing tolerance is −1.7 mm to +1.6 mm (usable shop rule ±1.5 mm).

'Population Arithmetic and the Supering Rule: When Storage Binds and What a Week of Delay Costs'. Its stated result: The cohort model peaks at 71,400 adults on day 122. At the stated nectar flow the brood box's 26,500 free cells bind in 4.77 days, giving the rule: super at 10 days of storage cover (55,556 free cells). Supering one week late costs 16.84 kg of honey — 5.57 kg never stored plus 11.26 kg forgone because backfilled brood cells remove 22,525 adults — and two weeks late costs 34.34 kg.

'What Drawn Comb Costs: The Honey Price of a Box of Comb and a Bound on Annual Comb Renewal'. Its stated result: At the stated 7.0 kg of honey per kilogram of wax, a box of comb costs 8.4 kg of honey foundationless against 2.8 kg on foundation and nothing for drawn comb — first-season penalties of 21.0% versus 7.0% of a 40 kg crop.

'Bad Air at the Bottom: A Ventilation Bound and a Test Rule for Hand-Dug Wells'. Its stated result: Without ventilation, the stated 0.5% concentration level is reached in 0.34 hours at 5 m, 0.68 hours at 10 m, 1.02 hours at 15 m, and 1.35 hours at 20 m; the stated 4.0% immediately-dangerous level is reached in 2.93 hours, 5.85 hours, 8.78 hours, and 11.70 hours at the same depths.

'Holding a Load with Two Fingers: The Capstan Rule for Well Work, and Where Wet Rope Breaks It'. Its stated result: Two wraps multiply a holding force by 43.38 in the dry-on-wood state, but by only 6.59 when the same rope is wet, by 12.35 on steel, and by 3.51 on wet steel. At the stated maximum one-person holding force of 150 N, two wraps therefore restrain at most 663.2 kg dry on wood, but only 100.7 kg wet on wood, 188.8 kg on steel, and 53.7 kg on wet steel.

'Chain or Rope: A Weight, Stretch, and Strength Accounting for Raising Water and Loads'. Its stated result: Chain weighs 18.33 times as much per metre as the polyester rope and 7.1 times as much as the manila rope. At a depth of 5 m the chain alone already weighs 11.0 kg, exactly the payload, and the total suspended mass is 22.0 kg; at 50 m the chain system totals 121.0 kg against 26.5 kg for manila and 17.0 kg for polyester, and the energy required for the lift is 32373.0 J for chain against 9196.9 J for manila and 6867.0

'The Counterweight Well: Sizing the Stone That Reduces the Work of Raising Water'. Its stated result: For the main case, an empty bucket of 3.0 kg carrying 15 kg of water raised through 10 m, the counterweight that minimises the peak force in the cycle is 10.5 kg, which equalises the two strokes at a peak force of 73.6 N, well below the unaided peak of 176.6 N.

'Sizing the Cylinder to the Well: A Force-Balance Rule for Hand-Pump Bore Diameter Against Depth'. Its stated result: Under the central assumptions — a sustainable handle force of 150 N, a lever ratio of 4, seal friction of 45 N, and a steel pump rod of 12 mm diameter weighing 8.709 N per metre — the maximum bore is 77.9 mm at a depth of 10 m, 49.7 mm at 20 m, 35.6 mm at 30 m, and 25.9 mm at 40 m.

'How Long to Reach Water: Excavated Volume, Hoisting Work, and Digging Time by Depth and Soil'. Its stated result: For the nominal shaft the excavated volume to a depth of 20 m is 22.62 m³, corresponding to spoil masses of 38.45 t in loose sand and gravel, 40.72 t in medium clay, 42.98 t in stiff clay, and 47.50 t in weathered rock and hardpan, moved in 1,301, 1,414, 1,470, and 1,583 bucket lifts respectively.

lesson.teach: Settle in. I am Professor Lorenzo Ribeiro, and this is The Market Stall (Wave 6). This class is built on real papers — deposited, citable work. I will present each paper and what it reports; that presentation is the lesson. At the end I will ask you questions on what was taught here — nothing else.

'Spoilage Against Selling Time: A Temperature-Dependent Decay Model for Leafy Greens and a Break-Even Rule for How Much to Bring to Market'. Its stated result: First, saleable fraction by temperature and age, with a half-life of 23.10 hours at 20 °C, falling to 9.24 hours at 30 °C and 5.85 hours at 35 °C. Second, a costing of unsold stock: at 30 °C, bringing 100 bunches against demand of 85 sells 80.23, loses 19.77 to spoilage, and carries an unsold cost of $23.73.

'End-of-Day Discounting for a Decaying Perishable: A Triggered Single-Markdown Schedule That Maximises Computed Revenue'. Its stated result: The originated result is a triggered, single-markdown schedule. At the midpoint, count the stock remaining. If it exceeds 39.6 bunches — 1.2 times the 33 bunches expected to sell at full price in the remaining three hours — apply one markdown of 20 percent for the rest of the day. Otherwise hold full price.

'Harvest Timing Against Market Timing: Quality-Loss Bounds for Morning-of and Evening-Before Harvest of Leafy Greens, and a Rule for When Each Wins'. Its stated result: At opening, morning-of retains 0.9576, 0.9339, 0.8974, and 0.8428 across those days — a loss of 4.2 to 15.7 percent. Evening-before at ambient retains only 0.7707, 0.6624, 0.5214, and 0.3571 — a loss of 22.9 to 64.3 percent. The cool box retains 0.8608 on every day, because its temperature does not depend on the weather. Two thresholds are originated.

'Stall Shading and Wilting: How Much Selling Time Shade Buys for Leafy Produce, and When It Pays'. Its stated result: On a typical day defined here as 30°C air temperature and 45% relative humidity, the modelled time to wilting is 2.756 hours in open sun, 3.287 hours under cloth transmitting 0.7 of the sun, 3.727 hours under cloth transmitting 0.5, and 4.259 hours under cloth transmitting 0.3. Medium shade, at transmission 0.5, therefore buys 0.971 hours, a gain of 35.2%.

'Display Height and Reach: The Reachable Fraction of a Market Stall and a Stepped Display Rule'. Its stated result: On a flat table 120 cm deep, only 0.3333 of the stock, uniformly distributed by depth, lies within customer comfortable reach, and only 0.5000 lies within customer maximum reach. The middle 30 cm is beyond comfortable reach from either side, although it can be reached at full stretch by someone. On a table 150 cm deep a dead zone appears: 20 cm in the middle is beyond maximum reach from either side.

'Stacking Depth and Crushing: Maximum Safe Depth for Ripe Tomatoes and the Cost of Exceeding It'. Its stated result: Under these assumptions each additional layer adds 1.65 N to the bottom fruit. Damage in the model begins well before the threshold is formally crossed: the bottom layer damage fraction is 0.0000 at six layers, 0.1378 at seven layers, and 0.2904 at eight layers, where the force is 11.54 N and the pressure is 65.3 kPa. At nine layers, a depth of 53.6 cm, the force reaches 13.18 N and exceeds the threshold.

lesson.teach: Settle in. I am Professor Richard Martin, and this is Household Manufactures (Wave 6). This class is built on real papers — deposited, citable work. I will present each paper and what it reports; that presentation is the lesson. At the end I will ask you questions on what was taught here — nothing else.

'A strength test for wood-ash lye without instruments'. Its stated result: The central egg, at 1.060 g/mL, reaches neutral buoyancy at 65.2 g/L of alkali as potassium carbonate, but eggs spanning 1.030 to 1.090 g/mL indicate anywhere from 32.6 to 97.8 g/L at the same visual point, a range 65.2 g/L wide against a target band only 40.0 g/L wide. An egg floating with 5% exposed corresponds to 125.9 g/L, near the top of the target band of 90.0 to 130.0 g/L.

'One recipe does not fit every fat'. Its stated result: A fixed recipe of 140.0 g of sodium hydroxide per kilogram requires, in fact, 99.1 g for lard and 182.5 g for coconut oil, a range whose maximum is 1.84 times its minimum. On tallow the fixed recipe leaves 39.5 g of surplus alkali per kilogram, a free alkali content of 3.06% in the cured bar, 30.6 times a 0.1% reference limit. On coconut oil it falls short by 42.5 g and leaves 23.3% of the fat unsaponified.

'The curing bound: when is a bar of soap actually ready?'. Its stated result: For a stated 120.0 g bar measuring 80 by 55 by 25 mm, starting at 28.0% water and curing at 20 °C and 50% relative humidity, water falls to 20.2% at day 7, 15.6% at day 14 and 11.3% at day 28. Free alkali in a zero-superfat batch falls from 2.40% at demoulding to 0.43% at day 7 and reaches 0.1% only at day 22.9.

'Sizing a solar salt pan'. Its stated result: For seawater at a mass fraction of 0.035, the rule gives 5.059 m2 of pan per kilogram of salt per day in an arid coastal climate with net evaporation of 5.45 mm per day, and 19.694 m2 per kilogram per day in a humid coastal climate with net evaporation of 1.4 mm per day.

'The break-even salinity for boiling brine'. Its stated result: Boiling seawater at a salt mass fraction of 0.035 requires 70.586 MJ of heat and 31.371 kg of wood for each kilogram of salt. At a mass fraction of 0.2 the cost falls to 10.491 MJ and 4.662 kg of wood, and at 0.26, near saturation, to 7.549 MJ and 3.355 kg of wood.

'Evaporate to dryness is worse salt'. Its stated result: Stopping at 7.0 g of water remaining recovers 24.48 g of NaCl, a recovery of 90.7 percent, at a dry-crystal purity of 0.9532, or 0.9163 after allowing for retained mother liquor. lesson.teach: Settle in. I am Professor Deepika Sharma, and this is Building with Local Materials (Wave 6). This class is built on real papers — deposited, citable work. I will present each paper and what it reports; that presentation is the lesson. At the end I will ask you questions on what was taught here — nothing else.

'Lime and Ash: What a Wood-Ash Pozzolan Mortar Can and Cannot Do'. Its stated result: Per 100 kg, wood ash carries only 3.0 kg of reactive silica against rice husk ash's 77.44 kg. Wood ash with water alone forms at most 8.73 kg of gel per 100 kg (0.78 MPa dry, 0.08 MPa wet), and wood ash with clay at 50:50 gives 0.49 MPa dry and 0.02 MPa wet, so neither belief survives the arithmetic.

'How Far Can a Bamboo Culm Span? Bending Strength and Deflection Bounds for Single and Bundled Culms'. Its stated result: Deflection at span/240 governs every case computed; bending strength never does. A single 100 mm culm under 250 N/m spans 3.96 m by deflection against 7.89 m by strength; bundling two culms reaches 4.89 m and three reach 5.48 m at the same load, and a 1,000 N midspan point load bounds the single 100 mm culm to 3.23 m.

'The Bamboo Column Bound: Safe Axial Load by Culm Diameter, Wall Thickness, and Node Spacing'. Its stated result: Safe axial load is the smaller of factored Euler buckling and crushing, with diameter and wall taken at mid-height: a 100 mm culm with a 10 mm wall carries 62.2 kN at 1.0 m unsupported length, 38.6 kN at 2.0 m, and 17.2 kN at 3.0 m.

'A Bolt Through a Bamboo Culm Does Not Use the Culm's Strength: Splitting and Bearing Bounds at Pinned Joints, and a Lashing Rule That Does'. Its stated result: A 12 mm through-bolt in a 100 mm culm with a 10 mm wall reaches an ultimate bearing load of 8.4 kN, which is 5.4% of the culm's crushing strength, and a safe transfer of only 2.8 kN. The selection rule that follows: a single lashing to 3.75 kN, a double lashing to 6.75 kN, a plugged bolt to 12.0 kN, and beyond that multiple joints rather than a stronger fastener.

'The Dry-Stone Retaining Wall Bound: Batter, Base Thickness, and the Height a Vertical Face Cannot Reach'. Its stated result: A vertical dry-stone face needs a base of 0.58 times the retained height; a 1-in-6 batter needs 0.538 times the height with about a fifth less stone. At equal stone volume and 3.0 m retained height, the battered wall's overturning factor is 3.857 against the vertical wall's 3.010, a 28.1% gain; under a 1.50 m base cap the battered face reaches 2.75 m, a height the vertical face cannot reach.

'Foundation Width from the Ground Up: A Bearing Rule for Stone Strip Footings'. Its stated result: Wall, roof, and floor loads are accumulated openly — 35.16 kN/m for a cottage, 71.82 kN/m for a two-storey stone house — and the footing width is the larger of the bearing width and wall thickness plus 0.30 m.

I will present each paper and what it reports; that presentation is the lesson. At the end I will ask you questions on what was taught here — nothing else.

'Dose Past the Demand, Then Mind the Calendar: Chlorine, Contact Time, and Re-Dosing for Stored Roof Water'. Its stated result: A 1.0 mg/L chlorine dose in water with a demand of 1.5 mg/L leaves no free residual and disinfects nothing at any waiting time; the typical case (demand 0.8 mg/L, dose 2.0 mg/L, residual 1.2 mg/L, 40 mL of 5 percent bleach per 1,000 L) reaches the bacterial CT target of 15 mg·min/L in 12.5 minutes, and its protection lasts 35.8 days in a cool dark covered tank but only 4.5 days in a warm light-admitting one, so re-do

'Clean by the Mound, Not by the Calendar: A Sediment Accumulation Rule for Rainwater Cisterns'. Its stated result: Sediment concentrates near the inlet, so the typical tank (60 g/m²/yr, no first-flush diverter) builds local depth at 3.57 mm per year and reaches a 50 mm cleaning trigger in 14.0 years rather than the 70 years a whole-floor average suggests; intervals across load classes run from 4.2 years (ageing shingles, no diverter) to 117.6 years (clean metal roof, diverter fitted), a 28-fold spread, and a maintained diverter m

'A Barrier Is a Pump Specification: Hydrostatic Load, Sandbag Count, and Leakage at a Household Flood Door'. Its stated result: Floodwater 0.6 m deep exerts 1,589 N across a 0.90 m doorway — four times the 397 N at 0.3 m, because load grows with the square of depth — a sandbag wall for that duty takes about 93 bags per metre (roughly 139 for a doorway with returns), and even a well-compressed seal passes 11.1 L/min across the door at 0.6 m depth, so a barrier specification is incomplete without a leakage class and a matched pump.

'Counted, Not Placed for Symmetry: How Many Downpipes a Roof Actually Needs'. Its stated result: Counting downpipes from rational-method design flow rather than elevation symmetry: a 200 m2 roof at 150 mm/h produces 8.33 L/s and needs three 82 mm or two 110 mm downpipes, so the customary pair of 82 mm pipes is undersized, and every roof needs at least two outlets for blockage redundancy.

'The Drip Lands Further Out Than the Trench: Width, Wind, and Impact Energy at an Unguttered Eave'. Its stated result: Water leaving a 3.5 m eave lands 0.253 m from the wall in still air, so a trench must be 0.45 m wide once splash is allowed for, and the conventional 300 mm trench misses the drip line even with no wind; a 2 m/s wind raises the required width to 0.70 m, a 600 mm trench tolerates only about 1.55 m/s of wind at that height, and impact energy rises from 34.4 J per litre at 3.5 m to 68.7 J per litre at 7.0 m.

'One Millimetre for Every Roof? First-Flush Diversion Depth Set by Wash-Off Behaviour'. Its stated result: Against the exponential wash-off model, the popular fixed 1 mm first-flush rule captures only 19.7 percent of the load on a typical suburban roof; 90 percent capture needs 10.47 mm there and 19.19 mm under trees, while the extra diversion costs only a few percent of the annual harvest.

lesson.teach: Settle in. I am Professor Rahul Iyer, and this is Clay, Pottery and Kilns (Wave 7). This class is built on real papers — deposited, citable work. I will present each paper and what it reports; that presentation is the lesson. At the end I will ask you questions on what was taught here — nothing else.

'Chimney Height for a Downdraft Pottery Kiln: The Draft Pressure Needed and the Height Beyond Which Fuel Use Barely Falls'. Its stated result: A 3 m chimney gives the lowest fuel use in the sweep at 427.2 kg per firing (draft 22.3 Pa), 5.7 percent below a 2 m chimney (453.0 kg), while a 10 m chimney wastes fuel on excess draft at 514.6 kg per firing.

'Covered Drying for Green Bricks: How Much Roof per Thousand Bricks Keeps Rain Losses Below Fuel Savings'. Its stated result: Covering 60 percent of the drying yard minimises cost per batch of 10,000 bricks at USD 152.5, cutting rain losses from 2,200 bricks uncovered to 628, against USD 198.0 uncovered and USD 178.0 for full cover.

'Ceramic Water Filter Wall Thickness: The Flow and Pathogen-Removal Trade-Off and a Thickness That Meets Both Targets'. Its stated result: A 12 mm filter wall is the thinnest section meeting both stated targets at once, flowing 1.67 litres per hour with a log removal value of 3.36; a 6 mm wall flows 3.33 litres per hour but removes only 1.68 log, and an 18 mm wall reaches 5.04 log at 1.11 litres per hour.

'Wet Fuelwood and Kiln Fuel Bills: The True Fuel Mass Multiplier at Common Moisture Contents, Against the Claim That Wet Wood Burns Almost as Well'. Its stated result: The claim that wet wood burns almost as well as dry wood is disproved by evaporation arithmetic: effective heat falls from 15.94 MJ per kg at 10 percent moisture to 5.64 MJ per kg at 60 percent, so fuel mass must rise by a factor of 2.07 at 50 percent moisture and 1.35 at 30 percent to deliver the same heat.

'A Crazing-Free Window for Low-Cost Glazes: The Thermal Expansion Mismatch a Fired Glaze Can Tolerate on a Porous Earthenware Body'. Its stated result: The crazing threshold for the stated glaze is an expansion mismatch of 0.75 parts per million per degree C: at a mismatch of +1.0 the glaze stress reaches 46.7 MPa, above the 35 MPa tensile strength, while +0.5 gives 23.3 MPa and is the largest safe positive mismatch in the sweep.

'Rice Husk in Fired Bricks: Why More Husk Is Not Always Better, and the Blend That Best Balances Strength, Weight and Cost'. Its stated result: The claim that more rice husk always improves a brick does not survive the arithmetic: the scored optimum is a 0.10 husk fraction (strength 11.1 MPa), while at 0.30 the strength falls to 5.2 MPa, below the 7 MPa loadbearing threshold, even though density falls to 1152 kg per cubic metre.

'Bed Height for Older Sleepers: The Seat-Height Rule That Minimises Sit-to-Stand Effort, and the Fall Energy Cost of Exceeding It'. Its stated result: For a popliteal height of 42 cm, standing from a 45 cm bed top requires an effort index of 103.7, against 100.0 at the recommended height and 57.1 from a fashionable 65 cm top — the effort curve is steep below knee height and flat above it. Raising the top to 75 cm raises the energy of a roll-out fall for a 70 kg sleeper from 316 J at the recommended height to 515 J.

'Blackout Is a Gap Problem: Light at the Eye from Blind Edge Leakage as a Function of Gap Width, and the Overlap That Replaces Expensive Fabric'. Its stated result: With the gaps sealed, blackout fabric holds the eye to 0.15 lux; a gap of only 2.0 mm around the perimeter breaches a stated 1 lux design criterion, and a 10 mm gap admits 4.6 lux — more than an ordinary curtain with sealed edges delivers through its fabric at 7.5 lux. A simple overlap strip that forces gap light through two reflections cuts the 10 mm case to 0.32 lux.

'How Much Blanket Is Enough: A Tog Sizing Rule from Sleeping Heat Production, Room Temperature, and the Insulation Already Supplied by the Mattress'. Its stated result: The requirement falls from 15.5 tog at 10 degrees to 8.0 tog at 19 degrees and 5.5 tog at 22 degrees. A 13.5 tog duvet in a 19 degree room therefore carries 5.5 tog of surplus insulation, which in the model would drive mean skin temperature to 40.1 degrees if the sleeper did not respond by throwing it off.

'Dawn Simulation, Priced in Lux-Minutes: The Ramp Duration and Peak Illuminance a Wake-Up Light Needs at Realistic Pillow Distances'. Its stated result: At the bedside the peak is 300.0 lux and a 30-minute ramp delivers 4500 lux-minutes; across the room at 1.8 metres the peak collapses to 23.1 lux and the same ramp delivers 347 lux-minutes, far below a stated effective band of 2500 to 7500. Reaching the band's middle from across the room would need a ramp of 432.0 minutes.

'Heat the Bed or Heat the Room: The Energy Arithmetic of an Electric Blanket Against Night-Time Space Heating'. 'Hand-Mixed or Capsule: Glass Ionomer Waste and Restorations per Kit in Atraumatic Restorative Treatment'. Its stated result: Atraumatic restorative treatment depends on glass ionomer, bought either as powder and liquid for hand mixing or as pre-dosed capsules. This study compares the two routes at stated values: a restoration needs 0.20 g of mixed material; hand mixing prepares 0.35 g per attempt with 12 percent of mixes discarded for ratio failure; a capsule delivers 0.40 g with 2 percent failure.

'When a Toothbrush Stops Cleaning: A Splay-Based Replacement Rule and Its Cost per Effective Brush'. Its stated result: Toothbrush replacement is usually governed by habit or by a calendar printed on packaging, not by how well the brush still cleans. This study models plaque-removal efficacy as falling linearly by 0.045 per week of twice-daily use from an initial index of 1.00, and computes end-of-life and mean efficacy, brushes per year, and annual cost at a bulk price of USD 0.60 for replacement intervals from 2 to 16 weeks.

'Brushing with a Cup Instead of a Running Tap: Water Saved per Person and the Rinse Volume That Still Clears Paste'. Its stated result: Toothbrushing advice assumes a running tap and never prices the water. This study compares a running-tap routine (6 litres per minute for 45 seconds, 4.5 litres per brushing) with a single 200 mL cup, and checks the cup against a stated dilution model of paste clearance in which the residual fraction after rinsing with volume V is exp(-V/60).

'Charcoal Toothpaste and the Whitening Claim: Abrasive Wear per Shade Gained and the Fluoride the Claim Leaves Out'. Its stated result: Charcoal toothpastes are sold on a whitening claim. This study tests the claim against a stated saturating model of stain removal, in which any paste above an abrasivity index of 60 reaches the same shade gain of 1.90 shades at four weeks, and a stated wear model in which annual abrasive wear is proportional to the abrasivity index.

'A Smear, a Pea, or a Ribbon: Fluoride Dose per Brushing for Young Children and the Dispensing Rule That Keeps It in Range'. Its stated result: Advice on how much toothpaste a young child should use is given in pictures, a smear or a pea, without stating the dose those pictures deliver. This study computes fluoride applied and swallowed for three dispensing amounts (smear 0.10 g, pea 0.25 g, full ribbon 0.60 g), two paste strengths (1000 and 1450 ppm), and two age bands, with stated swallowed fractions and a stated upper intake criterion of 0.10 mg per kg pe

'Half a Tablet Cleans as the Label Fears It Might Not: Concentration, Soak Time, and Cost in Denture Cleansing'. Its stated result: Denture cleansing tablets are used one per soak by label instruction, and halving them is a common household economy of unknown effect. This study evaluates dose and soak time together under a stated concentration-time criterion of 3.0 normalised units, where a whole tablet in 150 mL defines a concentration of 1.00 and a half tablet 0.50.

lesson.teach: Settle in. I am Professor Fitri Le, and this is Household Pests and Stored-Goods Protection (Wave 8). This class is built on real papers — deposited, citable work. I will present each paper and what it reports; that presentation is the lesson. At the end I will ask you questions on what was taught here — nothing else.

'Bait Stations Along an Ant Trail: The Spacing at Which Discovery Time, Not Dose, Becomes the Limit'. Its stated result: Place liquid bait stations about 2 m apart along the active trail (nine stations for an 18 m trail, about USD 9.90 in hardware), refill weekly, do not spray the trail during baiting, and allow ten days before judging the attempt; on the stated assumptions the colony dose is complete in about 2.8 days at this spacing, and wider spacings fail mainly by delaying discovery.

'The Thick Mattress Problem: Heat-Soak Time Scales With the Square of Thickness in Bed Bug Room Treatments'. Its stated result: Plan the hold from the thickest item: at 60 C air, allow at least 4 hours for 10 cm of foam, 16 hours for 20 cm, and treat 30 cm items (36 hours) as impractical to clear in place — split, open or remove thick items so no conduction path exceeds about 10 cm, and verify with a probe in the core of the thickest remaining item.

'One Trap or Two? Detection Probability for a Light Clothes Moth Infestation in a Wool Store'. Its stated result: Hang two pheromone traps per small textile store room, at low level and at opposite ends, replace them every eight weeks (USD 12 per round), and treat any catch as a trigger to inspect and treat the textiles themselves; a third trap in the same room adds cost without detection.

'Gel Dots on a Grid: The Widest Spacing That Still Collapses a German Cockroach Population in a Kitchen'. Its stated result: Apply gel dots of about 0.1 g at no more than 1.1 m spacing along every harbourage line, counting each cabinet level separately (19 dots for 20 m of line, under USD 1 of gel), and re-apply at the same spacing after about three weeks; spacings of 3 m or more should be expected to fail outright, however much gel each dot contains.

'Warm Washes and Dust Mites: The Temperature Below Which No Practical Cycle Reaches a Three-Log Reduction'. Its stated result: Wash bedding intended as a mite control measure at 60 C with a normal-length cycle (about 24 minutes of allowance covers the 3-log target at the load's coldest point); treat 40 C washing as allergen-removal cleaning only, and use hot tumble drying, freezing or encasements for items that cannot be washed at 60 C.

'Vacuuming Against the Flea Life Cycle: The Interval Below Which a Carpet Reservoir Collapses Without Insecticide'. Its stated result: Vacuum the pet's resting and sleeping areas daily for the first 14 days of a flea infestation and every second day for the following 14, alongside effective treatment of the pet; weekly vacuuming should be expected to leave a breeding reservoir in place indefinitely.

lesson.teach: Settle in. I am Professor Jennifer Hall, and this is Paper, Ink, Books and Printing (Wave 8). This class is built on real papers — deposited, citable work. I will present each paper and what it reports; that presentation is the lesson. At the end I will ask you questions on what was taught here — nothing else.

'A Box That Buys Decades: Alkaline Reserve, Acid Migration and the Service Life of a Low-Cost Storage Box for Books and Papers'. Its stated result: A storage box board with a 3 percent alkaline reserve protects its contents for 12.0 years at 20 degrees Celsius and a high-buffer 8 percent board for 32.0 years, but the high-buffer board's life falls to 16.0 years in a 30-degree store, so reserve and cool storage together, not either alone, deliver decades of protection.

'Thick Book, Heavy Bill: Paper Bulk, Grammage and the Postage Cost of a Three-Hundred-Page Book'. Its stated result: For a 300-page A5 book, a 70 gsm bulky paper gives a 446 g book with a 16.8 mm spine, against 493 g and 14.4 mm for 80 gsm standard paper; against a 90 gsm standard paper the bulky choice also saves USD 0.80 per posted copy by staying in the lower postal band while looking thicker, not thinner.

'Four Pages at a Time: An Imposition Bound for A5 Booklets on A4 and A3 Sheets That Minimises Trim and Signature Waste'. Its stated result: An A5 booklet must contain a multiple of four pages: a 50-page text becomes a 52-page booklet with 2 blank pages (3.8 percent waste), a 32-page booklet needs exactly 8 A3 sheets, and at the stated sheet prices paper cost per booklet is identical on A3 and A4 stock, so the stock choice should be made on equipment and labour, not paper price.

'Carbon Ink That Stays in the Bottle and on the Page: Pigment Loading, Opacity and Settling Time for a Low-Cost Writing and Printing Ink'. Its stated result: For a carbon ink whose opacity saturates with pigment loading, 6 grams per litre is the lowest loading meeting the stated document optical density of 1.2, with a settling life of 113 days and a pen-safe viscosity, whereas 20 grams per litre raises density only to 1.83 while cutting settling life to 28 days.

'When Duplex Printing Saves Nothing: Reprint Losses, Jam Rates and the Net Paper Saving From Printing on Both Sides'. Its stated result: Duplex printing saves 49.8 percent of sheets with no user errors, 47.3 percent at a 5 percent reprint rate and 39.8 percent even at 20 percent errors; the saving is not exhausted until the reprint error fraction reaches 0.998, so duplex should be mandated for standard long documents and management effort spent on templates rather than on policing short jobs.

'The Longest-Lived Bar: Soap Bar Dimensions That Maximise Washes per Gram at Fixed Mass'. Its stated result: At 100 g the best grippable block found, 5.6 x 5.0 x 3.4 cm, lasted 916 washes, while the thinnest admissible slab lasted 417 washes and a typical oval approximated as a 22 mm thick tablet lasted 584 washes. The best block therefore delivers 56.8% more washes than the typical tablet from the same mass of soap, at a modelled cost of 0.1 US cents per wash against 0.15 cents.

'Buckets to a Safe Bath: A Mixing Ratio for Bath Water Without a Thermometer'. Its stated result: At a cold supply of 15 C, the exact ratio is 4.9 buckets of hot per 10 buckets of mixed water, and whole-bucket filling gives a bath at 36.5 C, inside the band. At 8 C the hot share rises to 5.6 buckets in 10 and at 22 C it falls to 3.9 in 10. Hot-supply drift of plus or minus 3 C moves the finished bath by plus or minus 1.3 C at the middle ratio.

'Keeping Shared Water Honest: The Exchange Rate a Communal Bath Needs to Hold a Stated Load Limit'. Its stated result: At six bathers per hour the exchange flow needed to hold the stated limit was 24 litres per hour, or 0.6% of the bath volume per hour. Stepped simulation reached a peak of 30000 units per litre, at the limit as designed. Session operation with a full change every 3 hours spent 74 minutes above the limit per session and used 8000 litres per operating day against 288 litres for continuous exchange.

'Warm Water Is Not the Active Ingredient: Energy Saved by Cold-Water Handwashing at Equal Modelled Removal'. Its stated result: Modelled removal at twenty seconds was 79.6% at 15 C and 87.5% at 40 C, a difference of 7.9 percentage points across the whole practical range, and 83.7% at 25 C. Heating the wash water to 35 C cost 71.9 kWh and USD 10.79 per household per year at the stated use, for that difference.

'Hard Water Eats Detergent: A Dosing Rule for Washing Cloth Nappies by Water Hardness Band'. Its stated result: The hardness tax alone was 14.8 g in soft water and 74.2 g in hard water, a difference of 59.4 g before any cleaning began. Total recommended doses were 42.8 g (soft), 72.5 g (moderate), 102.2 g (hard) and 136.9 g (very hard).

'Soap That the Garden Can Forgive: A Sodium Budget for Reusing Bath Water on Plants'. Its stated result: The baseline household applied 98.6 g of sodium per square metre per year before leaching, or 69.0 g net, against the stated ceiling of 12 g, an exceedance of 5.8 times. Halving bathing soap events reduced the net load to 34.5 g, still above the ceiling.

'Which Categories Belong in Cash? A Selection Rule for Envelope Categories Based on Overspend and Transaction Counts'. Its stated result: Pricing stated card-overspend factors against cash's hassle and forgone cashback, cash envelopes pay for online impulse purchases (net USD 563.33 a year), dining (USD 711.75) and entertainment (USD 277.20), but lose money on transport extras (USD -32.67); the selected set is worth USD 2093.68 a year.

'Cashback Against Interest: The Payoff Fraction Below Which a Rewards Card Costs More Than It Returns'. Its stated result: Simulating USD 1,400 a month on a 1.5% cashback card at 24.9% APR, the break-even payoff fraction is 59%: at 90% payoff the household carries a steady USD 159.15 balance and loses money net, and one month's spending carried for three months costs USD 88.97 of interest, erasing 4.2 months of cashback.

'The Coin Jar Examined: What a Year of Hoarded Change Costs Against Even a Modest Deposit Rate'. Its stated result: A USD 1.85-a-day change stream kept in a jar at home holds USD 5376.49 after ten years against USD 8291.54 if swept monthly into a 4.0% account — a gap of USD 2915.05, or 43.1% of contributions, with the three-year gap at USD 364.34 confirmed by stochastic simulation (median USD 500.92).

'How Many Months Is Enough? Emergency Fund Size Against the Duration of Income Interruptions'. Its stated result: Against a stated interruption process (4% monthly onset, 30% income continuation, essential spending USD 2600), a three-month emergency fund is exhausted in 21.8% of interruptions; 7 months brings exhaustion under 5% and 7 months under 1%, with a 99.2% chance of at least one interruption per decade.

'Setting the Cash Envelope: A Quantile Rule for Weekly Discretionary Caps That Bounds Overspend Without Starving Ordinary Weeks'. Its stated result: Setting a weekly discretionary envelope at the 90th percentile of desired spending (USD 250.99 for a distribution with mean USD 180 and standard deviation USD 55) limits breaches to about one week in ten, with a mean excess of USD 32.31 at the nearest tabulated cap and monthly exhaustion of a USD 150 buffer in 1.2% of months, whereas a cap at the mean is exceeded in 50.4% of weeks.

'How Often Must an Address List Be Re-Canvassed? Household Churn and the Cost of Stale Addresses'. Its stated result: An address list begins rotting the day it is finished: households move, buildings appear and vanish, names change. This paper prices that decay against the cost of repairing it. 'Albedo Modification to Amplify the Yarkovsky Effect on a 50-Metre Asteroid Over Twenty Years'. Its stated result: This paper computes the deflection obtained by changing the surface albedo of a 50 m asteroid of mass 111,264,740 kg so as to amplify its natural thermal recoil acceleration from 6.72e-13 to 3.02e-12 m per second squared, an enhancement factor of 4.5, using 1,200 kg of coating applied over 62 percent of the surface.

'An Anchored Chemical Propulsion Tug: A Short, High-Thrust Push on a 75-Metre Asteroid'. Its stated result: This paper computes an anchored chemical tug that pushes a 75 m asteroid of mass 618,501,054 kg using propellant carried from Earth. At a specific impulse of 322 s the rocket equation requires 5,320.0 kg of propellant, which is 0.00086 percent of the body's mass, to deliver the required 27.2 mm per second for a 6,000 km displacement with five years of warning. 'Compact Geostationary Microwave Power for an Island Direct-Current Microgrid'. Its stated result: Operating principle: A right-sized geostationary photovoltaic station transmits at 5.8 gigahertz to a single rectenna that feeds an island direct-current microgrid directly, matching the rectenna's native direct-current output to distribution without an inversion stage for local loads.

'Direct Solar-Pumped Laser Station Beaming to a Ground Receiver'. Its stated result: Operating principle: Sunlight collected by a large primary mirror pumps a laser medium directly, with no photovoltaic or electrical stage in space; the resulting beam near 1.06 micrometres is received on the ground by wavelength-matched photovoltaic converters.

'Geostationary Laser Power Beaming to a Dedicated Photovoltaic Receiver Farm'. Its stated result: Operating principle: A geostationary photovoltaic array drives solid-state lasers near 1.07 micrometres, and the narrow optical beam is received by photovoltaic cells tuned to that single wavelength rather than by a radio-frequency rectenna.

'Geostationary Microwave Phased-Array Solar Power for Continuous Baseload Delivery'. Its stated result: Operating principle: A geostationary photovoltaic array converts sunlight to direct current, feeds a 2.45 gigahertz phased-array transmitter, and beams microwaves to a large ground rectenna that converts the radio-frequency power back to direct current for the grid.

'Highly Elliptical Orbit Microwave Solar Power for High-Latitude Winter Supply'. Its stated result: Operating principle: Stations in highly elliptical Molniya-type orbits, dwelling for hours over the northern hemisphere near apogee, transmit at 2.45 gigahertz to a subarctic rectenna that receives little useful sunlight of its own in winter.

'Inflatable Concentrator Photovoltaic Station with Microwave Downlink'. Its stated result: Operating principle: Inflatable reflective troughs concentrate sunlight by a factor of about one hundred onto narrow strips of high-efficiency cells, shrinking the expensive semiconductor area by two orders of magnitude while a 5.8 gigahertz transmitter beams the power to a medium rectenna.

Operating principle: a steady superpressure platform holds a lidar at fixed altitude for weeks, profiling winds and temperatures above mountain wave sources so gravity-wave propagation into the stratosphere can be measured continuously

Operating principle: a carrier balloon climbs once and releases several unpowered gliders and falling sondes, each of which trades the balloon's altitude for range or for a vertical profile on the way down

'A Night-Only Cryogenic Telescope Balloon Sized by Cryogen Hold Time, Night Lift and Radiative Cooling Budgets'. Its stated result: Headline result: Frost Lantern holds its 4 K detector stage for 5.9 days on 420 litres of cryogen boiling off at 58 litres per day, while 390 kg of ballast protects 2.1 night observing cycles at 35.0 km.

Its stated result: Headline result: Each Drift Census unit lifts 330 g suspended on 363 g gross lift at 13.5 km, and 120 such units reporting every 10 minutes build the wind census over 48 days. Operating principle: many inexpensive small balloons, each lifting only a lightweight tracker, drift with stratospheric winds for weeks and report position by radio, so the fleet maps wind fields by its collective motion

'A Corrected Low-Cost Indoor Particle Witness: Humidity, Coincidence and Scattering Corrections for Classification Against the WHO 24-Hour PM2.5 Guideline, Below US$60'. Its stated result: Correcting a low-cost indoor particle counter for humidity, coincidence and scattering raises its simulated correct classification against the WHO 24-hour PM2.5 guideline from 81.8% to 89.7% across six non-fog home scenarios at a component total of US$55.50, but at fog-level humidity it classifies at only 49.8% and must not be trusted.

'A Disaster Mesh Communications Budget for a Town Without Grid or Towers: Coverage, Traffic, Power and Price for the First Week'. Its stated result: A solar LoRa-class mesh of 8 relays and one handset per household can carry a 7500-household town's coded first-week traffic (11,796 messages per day) at 0.989 delivery and $42.91 per covered household, but shadowed districts need 24 m relays at the slowest rate and the single-channel backhaul collapses below 90% delivery above 29,057 messages per day.

'A Flood Witness Network for the Settlements That Flood First: Design and a Computed Lead-Time Law for Low-Cost River and Rain Gauge Nodes at US$94 per River Node'. Its stated result: A network of US$94.00 river nodes spaced 5 km apart is computed to buy 75 minutes of warning on a 200 km² catchment at slope 0.003 at US$1.35 per warned household per year over five years, but buys no usable river-gauge warning on a 10 km² catchment, where only evacuation of people under a rain-based watch is served (SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED).

'A Flood Witness for Low-Water Road Crossings: Computed Warning Time, Sensor Placement and the False-Closure Trade-Off'. Its stated result: A solar-powered crossing witness delivers 15.28 minutes of warning on a small steep catchment at a ten-year cost of US$2,472.08 per crossing, but only 1.67 minutes on the smallest steep catchments, where a physical barrier — not a beacon — is the answer.

'A Heat Witness for Outdoor Workers: An Honest Error Bound for Cheap Heat-Stress Estimation'. Its stated result: With modern measured astrophysical factors, the "we are alone" outcome is not forced by the data — 99.7% of the spread in N comes from the four factors that remain unmeasured guesses, with longevity alone contributing 55.2%.

'The Life Term, Widened: What Relaxing the Carbon-and-Water Assumption Does to the Fermi Conclusion'. lesson.teach: Welcome in. I am Professor Eleanor Whitfield, and this is Numbers and Proof — the class where mathematics stops being arithmetic you were handed and becomes reasoning you can check. We begin with counting, because everything else is built on it and almost nobody examines it.

By the fourth week you will prove things — really prove them — first directly, then by contradiction, then by induction, which is a ladder you climb once and trust forever. Bring a pencil and a suspicious mind. If a step in my argument does not convince you, your job is to say so, out loud, in this room. That is not rudeness here. That is the subject.
Unit 1 of 6: Counting and the natural numbers.
Unit 2 of 6: Integers, rationals, and why fractions behave.
Unit 3 of 6: Irrational numbers and the real line.
Unit 4 of 6: What a proof is: direct proof and contradiction.
Unit 5 of 6: Proof by induction — the ladder argument.
Unit 6 of 6: Sets, functions, and the language of mathematics.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: Prove, in your own words, that there is no largest natural number — then say exactly which step of your proof would break if you tried it on the integers between 0 and 1. The worked answer: Suppose there were a largest natural number, N. Then N + 1 is also a natural number, and it is larger — contradiction, so no largest exists. Between 0 and 1 the same trick fails at the first step: N + 1 leaves the set entirely, so the contradiction never forms. A proof is only as good as the ground it stands on.

lesson.teach: I am Professor Priya Raman. This is Geometry — Euclid's Workshop, and the word workshop is chosen carefully: in here, we build. Two thousand three hundred years ago Euclid took five postulates — five sentences he declined to prove — and raised all of classical geometry on them, theorem by theorem, like courses of brick.

We will do the same, with straightedge and compass in hand, because a construction you have performed is a theorem you understand in your fingers. In the final week we knock out the fifth postulate and watch the whole building lean into curved space — which is where, much later, Einstein will be waiting for you.
Unit 1 of 6: Points, lines, and the five postulates.
Unit 2 of 6: Triangles: congruence and similarity.
Unit 3 of 6: Circles and their theorems.
Unit 4 of 6: Constructions with straightedge and compass.
Unit 5 of 6: Area, volume, and the Pythagorean theorem proved three ways.
Unit 6 of 6: What happens when the fifth postulate falls: a first look at curved geometry.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: With straightedge and compass only, construct the perpendicular bisector of a line segment, and write one sentence explaining why every point on it is exactly as far from one end of the segment as from the other. The worked answer: Draw circles of equal radius from both endpoints; where they cross, above and below, join the crossings — that line is the bisector. Every point on it sits on both circles’ symmetry: the two triangles it forms with the endpoints are congruent, so the distances to the ends are equal. Equal radii in, equal distances out.

lesson.teach: I am Professor Felix Wagner — welcome to Algebra, the language of unknowns. Algebra begins the moment you let a letter stand for a number you do not yet know, and refuse to be frightened by it. An equation is a balance: whatever you do to one side, you do to the other, and the truth stays level.

We will solve, graph, factor, and finally meet the quadratic formula — not as a spell to memorise but as a machine you will watch being built from completing the square. By the end, an unknown will feel less like a wall and more like a door with the handle on your side.
Unit 1 of 6: Letters that stand for numbers.
Unit 2 of 6: Equations and the balance principle.
Unit 3 of 6: Linear equations and their graphs.
Unit 4 of 6: Quadratics: factoring and the formula.
Unit 5 of 6: Systems of equations.
Unit 6 of 6: Inequalities and absolute value.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: Solve 3x + 7 = 25, showing the balance step you use at each line. Then solve x² − 5x + 6 = 0 by factoring. The worked answer: 3x + 7 = 25 → subtract 7 from both sides: 3x = 18 → divide both sides by 3: x = 6. For the quadratic, find two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to −5: −2 and −3, so (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0, giving x = 2 or x = 3. Check both in the original — algebra trusts, and then verifies.

lesson.teach: Come in. I am Professor David Kim, and this is AI Fundamentals. Before anything else, we clear the fog: artificial intelligence is not magic, and it is not a mind in a box. It is machinery — mathematics, running at enormous scale, on data. Here is the whole secret in one sentence: a model is a function that was shown so many examples that its guesses became good. Training is the showing.

The course's second unit names the three ingredients every system in this department is built from. Data: the examples the system learns from. Parameters: the internal settings inside it — the knobs. Training: the showing — the long process of adjusting those settings against the examples until the guesses come out right.

Two acts, and the whole class turns on keeping them apart. Training is the showing: before the system ever meets you, its settings are adjusted over millions of examples. Prediction is the act: afterwards, one new case at a time, the system produces its guess. Training happens in the workshop. Prediction happens in the wild.

Everything else — the chatbots, the image makers, the agents you will meet in this department's later classes — is those ideas, arranged with increasing cleverness. In this class we learn the honest vocabulary: data, parameters, training, inference — and we learn where these systems are strong, where they are brittle, and why both are true at once. You will leave able to read any headline about AI and know, within a sentence or two, whether it is reporting or theatre. The course walks six units in order: 1. What 'artificial intelligence' actually names · 2. Data, parameters, and training: the three ingredients · 3. What a model is — a function with a memory of examples · 4. Prediction as the core act · 5. Where AI is strong, where it is brittle, and why · 6. The honest vocabulary: no magic, no menace. That map is the course's shape, and it is yours for reference — the questions at the end are on what this lesson taught, not on the map.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: In your own words, one paragraph: what is a model, and what did training do to it? Use one example from your own life where prediction — not understanding — was enough. The worked answer: A model is a function — a machine for turning inputs into outputs — whose internal settings (parameters) were adjusted, over millions of examples, until its predictions matched reality often enough to be useful. Training is that adjustment. A spam filter never understood a word of your email; prediction was enough, and knowing the difference between the two is the whole first lesson.

lesson.teach: In, in. AI & Computing waits for no one, and neither do we. I am Professor Sana Rahal, and this is Machine Learning I — How Machines Learn From Data — a class in AI & Computing at Exolex University. Here is the whole course, taught unit by unit, in order.
Unit 1 of 6: Examples in, rules out: the inversion of programming.
Unit 2 of 6: Features and labels: what the machine is shown.
Unit 3 of 6: The loss function: a number that says 'wrong, this much'.
Unit 4 of 6: Gradient descent: walking downhill in the dark.
Unit 5 of 6: Overfitting: memorising instead of learning.
Unit 6 of 6: Test data: the exam the model has never seen.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: Explain overfitting to a friend using a student and an exam. Two or three sentences, no jargon you cannot unpack. The worked answer: Overfitting is the student who memorised last year's exam answers instead of learning the subject: perfect on the questions already seen, helpless on new ones. The cure is the same in both cases — hold back questions the learner has never seen, and grade on those.

lesson.teach: Welcome. In this room, aI & Computing is learned by doing it, not by watching it. I am Professor Ye-Jin Kim, and this is Computing Foundations — How Computers Actually Work — a class in AI & Computing at Exolex University. Here is the whole course, taught unit by unit, in order.

Unit 2 of 6: The processor: a very fast, very literal clerk.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: A computer is 'just' counting with electricity — write four sentences on what has to be added to counting before you get a word processor. Keep every claim checkable. A word processor is those four, wearing a friendly face.

lesson.teach: Come in, and look up. I am Professor Ada Whitmore, and this is Architecture One — Seeing Like an Architect. Before we draw a single line, we learn to see, because most people have lived their whole lives inside buildings they have never actually looked at. A building is three things at once: a structure that stands up, a skin that keeps the weather out, and a set of decisions about how people will live and move inside it.

In this class you will learn the architect's three honest views — the plan, from above; the section, cut through; the elevation, face on — and you will learn to ask of any building the questions that unlock it: What holds it up? Where does the light come in? How do people move?

Architecture is the most public art and the slowest technology we have; a building is an argument about how life should go, made in material that outlives the arguer. By the end of this class, no building will ever be invisible to you again.
Unit 1 of 6: The architect's eye: proportion, rhythm, scale.
Unit 2 of 6: Plan, section, elevation: the three honest views.
Unit 3 of 6: Structure and skin: what holds it up, what meets the weather.
Unit 4 of 6: Light as a building material.
Unit 5 of 6: How people move: circulation and the life inside the plan.
Unit 6 of 6: Reading a real building, start to finish.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: Take one building you know well. In five sentences: what holds it up, where does the light come in, and how do people move through it? You are reading it now, not just remembering it. The worked answer: The worked answer is the reading itself, in order: name the structure (posts and beams? load-bearing walls? a frame?), name the light (which faces, which openings, what hours), name the path (door to stair to room). A building you can describe in those three sentences is a building you have begun to see like an architect.

lesson.teach: Mind the threshold. Architecture is bigger inside than it looks. I am Professor Jae-Hyun Yang, and this is Structures — How Buildings Stand — a class in Architecture at Exolex University. Here is the whole course, taught unit by unit, in order.
Unit 1 of 6: Loads: the weight of everything, including snow and people.
Unit 2 of 6: Compression and tension: push and pull.
Unit 3 of 6: Beams, columns, and the betrayal of the long span.
Unit 4 of 6: The arch and the dome: compression made beautiful.
Unit 5 of 6: Frames, trusses, and the skeleton idea.
Unit 6 of 6: Foundations: arguing with the ground.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: A beam sags more in the middle than at the ends. In your own words: where is the top of the beam being squeezed, where is the bottom being stretched, and why does that tell you what material the beam wants to be? The worked answer: The top fibres are in compression (squeezed), the bottom in tension (stretched), and the middle depth barely works at all — which is why steel, strong in tension, carries the bottom of a concrete beam as rebar, and why an I-beam puts its material at the top and bottom edges where the work is.

lesson.teach: Mind the threshold. Architecture is bigger inside than it looks. I am Professor Xia Sun, and this is The Blueprint — Reading and Drawing Plans — a class in Architecture at Exolex University. Here is the whole course, taught unit by unit, in order.
Unit 1 of 6: Scale: the drawing as a promise at a ratio.
Unit 2 of 6: The plan view: walls as lines, doors as swings.
Unit 3 of 6: Sections and elevations: the other two truths.
Unit 4 of 6: Symbols and conventions: the shared shorthand.
Unit 5 of 6: Dimensions: numbers that someone will build from.
Unit 6 of 6: From sketch to set: how a drawing becomes a document.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. lesson.teach: Come in. Architecture is a craft here, and crafts are learned by hand. I am Professor Antti Andersson, and this is History of Building — Pyramids to Skyscrapers — a class in Architecture at Exolex University. Here is the whole course, taught unit by unit, in order.
Unit 1 of 6: Stone on stone: Egypt, Greece, and the post-and-lintel world.
Unit 2 of 6: Rome: concrete, the arch, and building an empire.
Unit 3 of 6: The Gothic wager: height and light on a skeleton of stone.
Unit 4 of 6: Iron and the industrial century.
Unit 5 of 6: Steel, elevators, and the skyscraper bargain.
Unit 6 of 6: The modern argument: what a building owes its street.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: Pick one leap — the arch, Gothic structure, iron, or steel-and-elevator — and write four sentences: what became possible that was impossible the year before, and what did it cost? The worked answer: Take the arch: before it, openings were limited to what a single stone lintel could span; after it, Rome could roof baths, bridge rivers, and stack aqueducts across valleys. The cost was skill and centring — every arch is built twice, once in timber to hold it up while it learns to stand. Each leap in this course has that shape: a new possibility, paid for in a new kind of knowledge.

lesson.teach: Come in. I am Professor Sylvia Anand, and this is Biology One — the cell, where life starts. Every living thing you have ever seen — the oak, the whale, the person beside you — is either one cell or a society of them, and everything life does, it does first inside this microscopic room.

In this class we take the cell apart respectfully: the membrane, a border that decides what may pass; the mitochondria, burning fuel into the currency every process spends; and the great central workflow — DNA read into RNA, RNA built into protein, proteins doing nearly all the actual work of being alive. Then the miracle of bookkeeping: how a cell copies three billion letters of instruction and divides, faithfully, into two.
Understand the cell and the rest of biology — organs, species, ecosystems — becomes the same story at larger scale. We begin, as life did, small.
Unit 1 of 6: The cell: life's smallest self-running unit.
Unit 2 of 6: The membrane: a border with customs officers.
Unit 3 of 6: Energy: mitochondria and the currency of ATP.
Unit 4 of 6: DNA to protein: the central workflow.
Unit 5 of 6: Division: how one cell becomes two, faithfully.
Unit 6 of 6: Specialisation: how identical instructions build a body.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: In four sentences: why is a cell compared to a city, and where does the comparison break? Both halves matter. The worked answer: The comparison works for division of labour — power stations (mitochondria), borders (membrane), a library of plans (DNA). It breaks at intention: no mayor, no plan-reader with a mind; the city's order emerges from chemistry obeying physics, and that emergence, not the metaphor, is the wonder.

lesson.teach: In, in. Biology & Life Sciences waits for no one, and neither do we. I am Professor Trang Rahmawati, and this is Genetics — DNA, Inheritance, and Variation — a class in Biology & Life Sciences at Exolex University. Here is the whole course, taught unit by unit, in order.
Unit 1 of 6: Genes and alleles: the instruction and its editions.
Unit 2 of 6: Dominant, recessive, and the honest complications.
Unit 3 of 6: Meiosis: shuffling the deck on purpose.
Unit 4 of 6: Mutations: copying errors and their long consequences.
Unit 5 of 6: Reading a genome: what a sequence can and cannot tell you.
Unit 6 of 6: Genetic medicine: promise, evidence, and hype.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: Two parents, both carriers of a recessive trait neither shows. What fraction of their children would show it, on average — and why does 'on average' matter in a real family of three? The worked answer: One in four, on average: each child independently has a 1/4 chance of receiving both recessive copies. 'On average' matters because three children are not a statistic — a real family could have none, or all three; probability governs crowds, not cradles.

lesson.teach: Come in. Biology & Life Sciences is a craft here, and crafts are learned by hand. I am Professor Daniel Turner, and this is Evolution — The Story Written in Species — a class in Biology & Life Sciences at Exolex University. Here is the whole course, taught unit by unit, in order.
Unit 1 of 6: Variation first: the raw material.
Unit 2 of 6: Selection: the environment as editor.
Unit 3 of 6: Deep time and the fossil record's honest gaps.
Unit 4 of 6: Speciation: when one story becomes two.
Unit 5 of 6: Evidence lines: fossils, anatomy, embryos, molecules.
Unit 6 of 6: Evolution in the present tense: microbes, moths, and medicine.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: In your own words: why is 'survival of the fittest' a misleading summary, and what four-word replacement does this class use instead? The worked answer: It misleads because 'fittest' suggests the strongest or best, when the mechanism only requires heritable differences in reproductive success — the class's replacement is 'descent with modification, filtered': descent with modification names the process, and the filter is any environment, not a contest with a winner's podium.

lesson.teach: Come in. Biology & Life Sciences is a craft here, and crafts are learned by hand. I am Professor Aino Nilsson, and this is Ecology — Living Systems and How They Hold Together — a class in Biology & Life Sciences at Exolex University. Here is the whole course, taught unit by unit, in order.
Unit 1 of 6: Energy flow: sun to grass to grazer to grave.
Unit 2 of 6: Food webs: nobody eats alone.
Unit 3 of 6: Cycles: water, carbon, nitrogen, round and round.
Unit 4 of 6: Populations: growth, limits, and the carrying question.
Unit 5 of 6: Keystone species: small numbers, enormous leverage.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: Pick one species and list what it eats, what eats it, and one thing that would change for three other species if it vanished. That web is the lesson. Three species, three different kinds of debt — that is a food web thinking.

lesson.teach: Come in. I am Professor Jonathan Meyer, and this is Health One — your body, owner's manual. You are the only person who will live in your body for its entire service life, and most owners are never given the manual. This class is the manual.

We walk the systems the way a good mechanic walks a machine: the heart and its plumbing, pressure and flow; the lungs and the blood, trading gases at a border thinner than paper; the immune system, an army with a memory, which is why vaccines work; and the signals — nerves for speed, hormones for reach — that hold the whole enterprise in feedback loops tuned like thermostats. Two rules in my room.

First: knowledge here is for understanding, never for self-diagnosis — a classroom informs, it does not treat. Second: every claim gets its evidence asked after. Bodies are systems, and systems can be learned. We begin.
Unit 1 of 6: The systems at a glance: one body, eleven crews.
Unit 2 of 6: The heart and the plumbing: pressure, flow, return.
Unit 3 of 6: Lungs and blood: the gas exchange.
Unit 4 of 6: The immune system: an army with a memory.
Unit 5 of 6: Signals: hormones, nerves, and feedback loops.
Unit 6 of 6: Numbers worth knowing: what the common tests measure.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: Pick one feedback loop in your body — temperature, blood sugar, or thirst — and describe it in four sentences: the sensor, the signal, the response, and what 'back to normal' means. The worked answer: Blood sugar, worked: sensors in the pancreas read glucose; the signal is insulin (or its opposite, glucagon); the response is cells taking up sugar or the liver releasing it; 'back to normal' is a range, not a point — the loop hunts around a setting, which is why healthy numbers wobble instead of pinning.

lesson.teach: Welcome. In this room, health & Medicine is learned by doing it, not by watching it. I am Professor Sanna Hansen, and this is First Aid — What To Do Before Help Arrives — a class in Health & Medicine at Exolex University. Here is the whole course, taught unit by unit, in order.
Unit 1 of 6: The first minute: assess, shout, send.
Unit 2 of 6: Bleeding: pressure, elevation, tourniquets — the real order.
Unit 3 of 6: Choking: the blocked airway, adult and child.
Unit 4 of 6: The unconscious person: recovery position and CPR's shape.
Unit 5 of 6: Burns, breaks, and bites: the common three.
Unit 6 of 6: The kit: what a home should actually hold.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: Write, from memory, the order of actions for finding an adult collapsed and unresponsive — five steps, in order. Then check it against the unit. The order is the lesson. The worked answer: One: check response and shout for help. Two: send someone specific to call emergency services and fetch a defibrillator. Three: open the airway, check breathing for no more than ten seconds. Four: if not breathing normally, start compressions — hard, fast, centre of the chest. Five: use the defibrillator the moment it arrives, and follow its voice. Every step exists because the minutes before help arrives are the minutes that decide.

lesson.teach: Mind the threshold. Health & Medicine is bigger inside than it looks. I am Professor Francesca Ribeiro, and this is Nutrition — Fuel, Repair, and the Long Game — a class in Health & Medicine at Exolex University. Here is the whole course, taught unit by unit, in order.
Unit 1 of 6: Macros honestly: protein, fat, carbohydrate, and what each is FOR.
Unit 2 of 6: Micronutrients: small doses, large consequences.
Unit 3 of 6: Energy balance without mythology.
Unit 4 of 6: Reading a label like a detective.
Unit 5 of 6: Fad diets: the anatomy of a recurring miracle.
Unit 6 of 6: Eating for decades: the unglamorous evidence.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: Take one food label and write three sentences: what it wants you to notice, what it mentions quietly, and what it cannot tell you at all. The worked answer: Labels shout the fashionable virtue (low fat! high protein!), mention the sugar or sodium quietly in the small grid, and cannot tell you the only thing that finally matters — what the rest of your day and decade of eating looks like. A label describes a food; health describes a pattern.

lesson.teach: Sit down, open your notebook — health & Medicine rewards the prepared. I am Professor Mary Wilson, and this is Medicine — How Healing Works, and How Doctors Think — a class in Health & Medicine at Exolex University. Here is the whole course, taught unit by unit, in order.
Unit 1 of 6: Diagnosis as detective work: hypothesis and test.
Unit 2 of 6: The evidence ladder: anecdote to trial.
Unit 3 of 6: How drugs work: keys, locks, and side effects as logic.
Unit 4 of 6: Surgery: repair under anaesthesia's truce.
Unit 5 of 6: Prevention: the medicine nobody notices.
Unit 6 of 6: Talking with doctors: questions that get answers.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: A friend swears a remedy worked because they took it and got better. Write the two questions this class teaches you to ask — kindly, but exactly. The worked answer: First: what would have happened without it — most illnesses improve on their own, so recovery after a remedy is the weakest evidence there is. Second: has it been tested against doing nothing (or against a placebo) in people like you? The questions are kind because they protect your friend; they are exact because 'it worked for me' has launched a thousand useless cures.

lesson.teach: Boots on. I am Professor Carla Mendes, and this is Plumbing One — water in, water out. Every building you will ever enter is quietly running two rivers: one under pressure, bringing clean water to every tap, and one with no pressure at all, coaxing waste away downhill — and the whole craft lives in understanding that those two systems obey opposite rules. Supply is force; drainage is persuasion.

In this class you will learn the parts that run the show: the trap, which keeps sewer gas out of your kitchen with nothing but a cup of standing water; the vent, which lets drains breathe; the shutoff, which you will locate in any house within a minute before I am done with you.

We learn it the way the work teaches it: principles first, hands on everything, safety always — water is patient and electricity is not the only thing in a wall that can hurt you. A good plumber is an applied physicist who gets wet. Let us get to work.
Unit 1 of 6: The two systems: supply under pressure, drainage by gravity.
Unit 2 of 6: Pipe materials and what each is for.
Unit 3 of 6: Valves, traps, and vents: the small parts that run the show.
Unit 4 of 6: Reading a leak: where water has been.
Unit 5 of 6: The plumber's core tools and what 'hand-tight plus a quarter' means.
Unit 6 of 6: Safety and law: permits, shutoffs, and knowing your limits.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: A sink drains slowly and gurgles. In three sentences: what is the gurgle telling you, and which part of the system — supply, trap, or vent — do you suspect first, and why? The worked answer: The gurgle is air being pulled through the trap's water seal — the drain is asking for air it should be getting from the vent. Suspect the vent (or a partial blockage making the drain behave like one): supply is pressurised and silent about drainage, the trap holds water by design, but a starved vent makes every drain in the line breathe through its traps.

lesson.teach: Mind the threshold. Trades & Applied Skills is bigger inside than it looks. I am Professor Heru Ho, and this is Electrical I — Circuits, Safety, and the Panel — a class in Trades & Applied Skills at Exolex University. Here is the whole course, taught unit by unit, in order.
Unit 1 of 6: Voltage, current, resistance: the water analogy and its limits.
Unit 2 of 6: The circuit: a loop or it is nothing.
Unit 3 of 6: The panel: breakers as guardians.
Unit 4 of 6: Grounding and GFCI: safety written in copper.
Unit 5 of 6: Wire, load, and heat: why sizes matter.
Unit 6 of 6: The rules that keep you alive: test, lock, verify.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: A breaker keeps tripping on one circuit. In three sentences: what is the breaker telling you, and why is 'replace it with a bigger breaker' the one answer that can burn a house down? The worked answer: The breaker is reporting that the circuit draws more current than its wires can safely carry — it is a guardian tripping on purpose. A bigger breaker silences the guardian while the wires, sized for the smaller current, overheat inside the walls. The fix is to find the overload or the fault, never to fire the messenger.

lesson.teach: Good to see you. Today trades & Applied Skills earns its keep. I am Professor Agnieszka Kowalczyk, and this is Carpentry I — Measure, Cut, Join — a class in Trades & Applied Skills at Exolex University. Here is the whole course, taught unit by unit, in order.
Unit 1 of 6: Wood: grain, movement, and why boards cup.
Unit 2 of 6: Measuring and marking: the pencil is a precision instrument.
Unit 3 of 6: Saws and the honest cut.
Unit 4 of 6: Joints: where carpentry becomes joinery.
Unit 5 of 6: Fasteners: nails, screws, glue — and choosing.
Unit 6 of 6: Squareness: the diagonal test that never lies.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: You measure both diagonals of a rectangular frame and they differ by a centimetre. What does the frame look like, and which corner do you push? The worked answer: The frame is a parallelogram — racked out of square. Push the corner at the end of the LONGER diagonal toward the other side: shortening the long diagonal until the two agree makes all four corners true at once. Equal diagonals are the definition of rectangular; carpenters trust them more than their eyes.

lesson.teach: Mind the threshold. Trades & Applied Skills is bigger inside than it looks. I am Professor Eko Prasetyo, and this is Automotive I — How a Car Works and What Breaks — a class in Trades & Applied Skills at Exolex University. Here is the whole course, taught unit by unit, in order.
Unit 1 of 6: The four strokes: what the engine is actually doing.
Unit 2 of 6: The supporting cast: cooling, lubrication, electrical.
Unit 3 of 6: Brakes and tyres: where the car meets physics.
Unit 4 of 6: Sounds, smells, and leaks: the diagnostic senses.
Unit 5 of 6: Maintenance that matters and maintenance theatre.
Unit 6 of 6: Reading a mechanic's invoice like an owner.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: A car overheats only in traffic, never on the highway. In three sentences: what does that pattern point to, and why does the highway hide it? The worked answer: It points at airflow, not coolant: at highway speed the road itself forces air through the radiator, masking a dead or weak cooling fan; in traffic the fan is the only airflow there is, so its failure shows. Patterns are diagnoses half-finished — when a fault happens is often what the fault is.

lesson.teach: Sit down, open your notebook — trades & Applied Skills rewards the prepared. I am Professor Gabriela Rivera, and this is The House Systems — Heating, Cooling, and Keeping a Home Alive — a class in Trades & Applied Skills at Exolex University. Here is the whole course, taught unit by unit, in order.
Unit 1 of 6: The furnace and the heat pump: moving heat versus making it.
Unit 2 of 6: Ducts and airflow: the forgotten half of comfort.
Unit 3 of 6: The thermostat: a negotiator, not a switch.
Unit 4 of 6: Insulation and air sealing: the cheapest fuel.
Unit 5 of 6: Water heaters, sump pumps, and the basement cast.
Unit 6 of 6: The seasonal walk: what to check before each season checks you.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: Two identical houses, one with heating bills half the other's. List the three likeliest reasons, in the order a professional would check them. The worked answer: Air sealing first — holes to the attic and outside leak heated air continuously and cost little to close. Insulation second — thin attic insulation is the classic silent bill. The equipment third — an old or oversized furnace wastes fuel, but it is checked last because the first two are cheaper and more common. Envelope before machinery: that order is the trade's whole wisdom in one line.

lesson.teach: Bonjour, et bienvenue. Je suis Madame Colette Marchand, and in this room, French is not studied — it is spoken, from the very first minute, mistakes and all, because mistakes are how a language moves in. Today: the vowels, which in French are pure and do not slide; your first introductions; and the two pillar verbs, être and avoir, to be and to have, on which everything else will stand.
By the end of this lesson you will order coffee, give your name, and say where you live — en français. Repeat after me, and do not whisper. A language learned quietly stays quiet.
Unit 1 of 6: Sounds of French: vowels first.
Unit 2 of 6: Bonjour, je m’appelle… — introductions that work.
Unit 3 of 6: Être et avoir: the two pillars.
Unit 4 of 6: Numbers, days, and the café.
Unit 5 of 6: Questions: asking your way around Paris.
Unit 6 of 6: The present tense of regular verbs.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: Write five true sentences about yourself in French using être and avoir — for example "Je suis étudiant" or "J’ai un chien" — and read them aloud twice. The worked answer: Model answers: "Je suis débutant, mais je suis patient. J’ai un cahier et un stylo. Je suis content aujourd’hui." Notice: être for what you are, avoir for what you have — and "j’ai" contracts because avoir begins with a vowel sound. Say them aloud; the mouth learns faster than the eye.

lesson.teach: Re-bonjour. I am Professor Camille Renaud, and welcome to Français Two — the class where your French learns to talk about yesterday. Until now everything you said happened in the present; today we build the passé composé, the workhorse past tense: a helper verb, avoir or être, carrying a past participle, like a friend carrying the heavy end of a table. J'ai mangé — I ate. Je suis allé — I went.
With those two shapes you can tell the story of your whole day, and a person who can tell stories in a language is no longer a tourist in it. Allez — racontez-moi votre journée.
Unit 1 of 6: Talking about yesterday: the passé composé with avoir.
Unit 2 of 6: Verbs that travel with être.
Unit 3 of 6: The imperfect: how things used to be.
Unit 4 of 6: Future plans: aller + infinitive and the futur simple.
Unit 5 of 6: Opinions, preferences, and polite disagreement.
Unit 6 of 6: A full conversation, start to finish.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: Write four sentences about what you did yesterday, in the passé composé: two with avoir, two with être (aller, venir, arriver, partir…). The worked answer: Model: "Hier, j’ai travaillé le matin et j’ai lu un livre. Je suis allé au marché, puis je suis rentré à la maison." Avoir carries most verbs; être carries the verbs of coming and going — and with être, the participle agrees: "elle est allée".

lesson.teach: Come in, and bring a sentence you love. I am Professor James Whitaker, and this is English Grammar and the Sentence. Grammar is not a set of traps laid by examiners; it is the engineering of English, the load-bearing structure under every sentence you will ever write or speak.

We will name the parts of speech, find the subject and verb hiding in long sentences like actors in a crowd, and learn punctuation as what it truly is: traffic signals for the reader's eye. You will read aloud in this room — everyone does — because a sentence you cannot say smoothly is a sentence that is not finished. Curtain up.
Unit 1 of 6: The parts of speech, without tears.
Unit 2 of 6: Subjects, verbs, and the complete thought.
Unit 3 of 6: Clauses: independent, dependent, and runaway.
Unit 4 of 6: Punctuation as traffic signals.
Unit 5 of 6: Agreement, tense, and pronoun discipline.
Unit 6 of 6: Editing a broken paragraph back to health.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: Take this broken sentence — "Running down the street, the bag fell open and the letters scattered everywhere" — name the fault, and rewrite it so the grammar carries the meaning. The worked answer: The fault is a dangling modifier: "running down the street" grammatically attaches to "the bag", and bags do not run. Rewrite: "Running down the street, I dropped the bag; it fell open and the letters scattered everywhere." Now the runner is a person, and the sentence stands up straight.
