lesson.teach: I am Professor Amara Okafor. This is Literature — Stories That Built the Language. We will not skim a hundred books in this room; we will read a few great ones slowly, aloud, the way they were built to be heard. Shakespeare first — one play, taken at walking pace, until the four-hundred-year-old jokes land again.

Then Austen, who taught the novel to think in two voices at once; then poetry, where sound itself carries the sense; then the short story, the most honest machine in literature. A story survives because every generation finds itself inside it. Your task this term is to find where you are standing in each one.
Unit 1 of 6: Why stories survive: the test of rereading.
Unit 2 of 6: Shakespeare: one play, read slowly.
Unit 3 of 6: The novel arrives: Austen and the free indirect voice.
Unit 4 of 6: Poetry: sound carrying sense.
Unit 5 of 6: The short story: Chekhov’s gun and other honest machinery.
Unit 6 of 6: Modern voices and where literature goes next.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: Choose any scene from the play we are reading. In five sentences: what does each character on stage want, and what is stopping them getting it? The worked answer: A strong answer names wants, not events. Example shape: "She wants the letter delivered before dawn, because everything she has planned depends on it. He wants to delay her, politely, because her success is his ruin. Neither can say so — the room is full of witnesses — so the want goes underground and comes out as manners." Want plus obstacle is the engine of every scene ever written.

lesson.teach: I am Professor Henry Walsh, and this is Composition — Saying It Plain. Orwell gave the whole course in one line: never use a long word where a short one will do. Plain writing is not simple-minded writing; it is the hardest kind, because nothing hides.

We will build paragraphs that land one idea at a time, structure arguments a busy reader can follow at speed, and practise cutting — every draft you bring me leaves ten percent lighter. Bring me your worst paragraph on the first day. We will make it stand up straight, and then we will make it walk.
Unit 1 of 6: The plain sentence as a discipline.
Unit 2 of 6: Paragraphs: one idea, fully landed.
Unit 3 of 6: Structure: opening, argument, close.
Unit 4 of 6: Cutting: the ten-percent rule.
Unit 5 of 6: Writing for a reader who is busy.
Unit 6 of 6: The essay: a position defended in the open.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: Write one paragraph — five sentences at most — arguing for something you genuinely believe. Then cut twenty percent of its words without losing any of its meaning, and hand in both versions. The worked answer: The cut version almost always wins by removing throat-clearing ("I think that", "in my opinion"), dead adverbs, and any sentence that repeats its neighbour in grander words. If a word can leave without the meaning limping, it was luggage, not cargo.

lesson.teach: In, in — stand up straight and breathe with me. I am Professor Rosa Delgado, and this is Singing One. Your voice is not something you either have or don't have; it is an instrument you already own and have simply never been taught to play. We start with breath, because breath is the engine under every note you will ever sing, then posture, then the great first skill: hearing a pitch and matching it, cleanly, without sliding.
You will sing in this room from the first day — briefly, kindly, and together — because the ear learns by doing, never by being described to. Pronti? Breathe in. Now — sing me that note back.
Unit 1 of 6: Breath: the engine under the note.
Unit 2 of 6: Posture and the open throat.
Unit 3 of 6: Finding pitch: matching a tone.
Unit 4 of 6: Intervals you can hear: seconds, thirds, fifths.
Unit 5 of 6: Vowels and diction while singing.
Unit 6 of 6: Your first song, performed in this room.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: Practise the five-note scale (do re mi fa sol) on one breath, three times a day. Then record yourself matching three single piano or app tones, and write down which was hardest to match and why you think so. The worked answer: Most people find the highest tone hardest: the breath runs thin and the pitch sags flat. The fix is not pushing — it is a taller posture and a slower, fuller breath before the note. Pitch problems are usually breath problems wearing a disguise.

lesson.teach: I am Professor Jonas Lindberg — welcome to Music Theory, the class that answers the question every listener has asked: why does that song work? Twelve notes are all we get, and everything — every anthem, every lullaby — is arrangement.

We will learn the staff, build the major scale from its pattern of whole and half steps, stack notes into chords, and take apart the famous one-four-five progression that powers a thousand songs, so you can hear the machine running under the music. Theory is not the enemy of feeling. It is feeling, with the lights turned on. By the end of term, no chord change will sneak past you ever again.
Unit 1 of 6: The staff and the twelve notes.
Unit 2 of 6: Major scales: the pattern of whole and half steps.
Unit 3 of 6: Intervals and how they feel.
Unit 4 of 6: Chords: triads built in thirds.
Unit 5 of 6: The I–IV–V engine of a thousand songs.
Unit 6 of 6: Minor keys and borrowed sadness.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: Build the C major scale and name its notes. Then build the three primary chords — I, IV, and V — and write out which scale notes each chord contains. The worked answer: C major: C D E F G A B C — no sharps, no flats, the pattern W-W-H-W-W-W-H. Chord I (C major): C-E-G. Chord IV (F major): F-A-C. Chord V (G major): G-B-D. Those three chords, in that family, carry most of the songs you have ever loved.

lesson.teach: I am Professor Keisha Thompson. Rhythm and Ear Training — the class your feet attend as much as your ears. Rhythm is the oldest part of music; there were drums long before there were melodies, and a song with perfect notes and a wandering beat is a speech with the words in the wrong order.

We will find the pulse in everything, clap in two and in three, meet syncopation — the note that arrives early on purpose and makes you move — and train the ear to name intervals by the songs they hide in. Homework in this class can be done walking, and I will know if you skipped it. Your feet will tell me.
Unit 1 of 6: Pulse: finding the beat in anything.
Unit 2 of 6: Note values and simple time.
Unit 3 of 6: Syncopation: the note that arrives early on purpose.
Unit 4 of 6: Clapping patterns in two and three.
Unit 5 of 6: Hearing intervals by their songs.
Unit 6 of 6: Dictation: writing down what you hear.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: Clap a steady pulse and count it in 4/4 for one minute without speeding up. Then clap the same pulse in 3/4. Write two sentences on how the two counts feel different in your body. The worked answer: In 4/4 the weight lands squarely, like marching: ONE two three four. In 3/4 it rolls: ONE two three, ONE two three — a waltz lean. If your 4/4 sped up, your pulse was chasing your excitement; anchor it by breathing out on beat one.

lesson.teach: Take a seat. The past is about to argue with the present. I am Professor Samuel Adeyemi, and this is World History — from river valleys to railways. We begin where civilisation begins: beside rivers, where farming first let people stay in one place long enough to build cities, argue about gods, and invent writing to keep track of the grain.

Everything after is the same story at larger scale — empires and the roads that held them, faiths that crossed oceans, revolutions that crossed everything. I will give you dates, because dates are anchors, but hear me: the dates are not the cargo. The cargo is people, deciding — often badly, sometimes magnificently — what to do next. That is what we study here.
Unit 1 of 6: River valleys: farming, cities, and the first states.
Unit 2 of 6: Empires and the roads that held them.
Unit 3 of 6: Faiths, philosophies, and the examined life.
Unit 4 of 6: Trade winds: goods, germs, and ideas.
Unit 5 of 6: Revolutions: political and industrial.
Unit 6 of 6: The twentieth century in one hard look.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: Pick one river-valley civilisation (Nile, Mesopotamia, Indus, Yellow River). In six sentences: what did the river give them, what did it demand of them, and what did they build because of both? The worked answer: Strong answers pair gift with demand. Egypt: the Nile gave predictable floods and rich silt — and demanded a calendar, surveying, and a state organised enough to manage both; what rose from that pairing was bureaucracy, monumental building, and three thousand years of continuity. Gift, demand, response: that triangle explains more history than any list of kings.

lesson.teach: I am Professor Nathan Cole. American History — the Republic's Argument With Itself, and I chose that title because it is the literal truth: this country was founded in an argument, written down in a constitution, and it has been arguing ever since about what its own words mean.

We will follow that argument from the colonies to the present — through expansion and its price, through a civil war when the argument turned violent, through industry, depression, and world wars. I am not here to hand you a verdict on America, favourable or otherwise. I am here to make you able to argue about it with the evidence open on the table. That is a citizen's skill, and it is learnable.
Unit 1 of 6: Colonies and the road to independence.
Unit 2 of 6: A constitution: the argument written down.
Unit 3 of 6: Expansion, and its price.
Unit 4 of 6: Civil war: the argument turns violent.
Unit 5 of 6: Industry, immigration, and the new century.
Unit 6 of 6: Depression, world wars, and the American century.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: Read the preamble of the Constitution — all fifty-two words. Choose the three words you think carry the most weight, and defend each choice in two sentences. The worked answer: A defensible set: "We" (who is included in the author of this document?), "Union" (the thing being made more perfect — the document admits imperfection at its start), and "posterity" (the audience is the unborn; the argument is addressed to the future). Any three words can win if the defence is honest — marks go to the reasoning, not the choice.

lesson.teach: Bring me a sentence you love. I am Professor June Calloway, and this is Writing One — The Clear Sentence. Everything you will ever write — letters, arguments, stories, applications that decide your life — is built from sentences, and a sentence has one job: to carry an idea from your mind into a stranger's without spilling it.

We will put strong verbs back in charge, cut the adverbs that lean on them like drunks on a lamppost, and learn rhythm — the long sentence and the short one, played against each other like music. Revision is not punishment here; revision is the writing. The first draft is just you telling yourself the story.
Unit 1 of 6: What a sentence is for.
Unit 2 of 6: Verbs that carry weight.
Unit 3 of 6: Cutting the fat: adverbs and throat-clearing.
Unit 4 of 6: Rhythm: long and short sentences together.
Unit 5 of 6: The paragraph as a room the reader walks through.
Unit 6 of 6: Revision: writing is rewriting.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: Write one sentence about something you did today, using the strongest verb you can find. Then write it again with the verb weakened by an adverb — and note, honestly, what was lost. The worked answer: Strong: "I tore the letter open." Weakened: "I quickly opened the letter." The strong verb carries speed, appetite, and feeling inside itself; the weak pair needs an adverb as a crutch and still says less. Verbs are the engine; adverbs are usually an apology for the engine.

lesson.teach: I am Professor Ingrid Sørensen. Storytelling — Structure, Scene, and Voice. Every story you have ever loved has the same skeleton under it: someone wants something, the world declines to hand it over, and the wanting changes them.

We will learn to see that skeleton — setup, turn, landing — then put meat on it: scenes that happen in front of the reader instead of being reported, dialogue that does two jobs at once, and voice, which is simply the sound of one particular mind on the page. Bring a story you cannot forget. By the end of term you will know exactly why you cannot forget it — and you will be dangerous with a pen.
Unit 1 of 6: The shape of stories: setup, turn, landing.
Unit 2 of 6: Scene versus summary.
Unit 3 of 6: Characters who want something.
Unit 4 of 6: Dialogue that does two jobs at once.
Unit 5 of 6: Voice: the sound of a mind on the page.
Unit 6 of 6: Endings that earn their feeling.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: Take a true event from your own life, small as you like. Write it twice: once as summary ("Then I went home and…"), once as a scene with dialogue. Four sentences each. Which one makes a reader feel something, and why? The worked answer: The scene wins, almost every time — because the reader is present for it. Summary tells the reader what happened; a scene lets it happen to them. Dialogue does the heaviest lifting: two lines of speech can carry character, conflict, and feeling that a paragraph of summary can only describe from outside.

lesson.teach: Come in. I am Professor Andre Boateng, and this is Business One — what a business is, from the ground up. Strip away the logos and the language and a business is one honest exchange: something of value, made or done, traded for money, with both sides glad it happened.

Everything else is machinery around that exchange — finding the customers, setting the price, watching the costs, and above all watching the cash, because businesses rarely die of unpopularity; they die of an empty account on a Friday with wages due.

In this class we build the whole picture plainly: what a customer actually buys (it is never quite the object), the margin between cost and price where a business lives, the legal shapes a business can wear, and the records it must keep — a business that cannot remember itself cannot be run, sold, or saved. Ambition is welcome here. Arithmetic is compulsory. Let us begin.
Unit 1 of 6: The exchange at the centre: value for money, both sides glad.
Unit 2 of 6: Customers: who they are and what they actually buy.
Unit 3 of 6: Costs, price, and the margin between them.
Unit 4 of 6: Cash flow: profit's faster, stricter sibling.
Unit 5 of 6: The legal shapes: sole trader, partnership, company.
Unit 6 of 6: Records: the memory a business keeps of itself.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: A business is profitable on paper and still dies. In three sentences: what kills it, and what number should its owner have watched every week? The worked answer: Cash flow kills it: profit can sit in unpaid invoices and stock on shelves while rent, wages, and suppliers demand actual money on actual dates. The number to watch weekly is cash — what is in the account, what is owed in, what is owed out, and when. Profit is an opinion at year-end; cash is a fact every Friday.

lesson.teach: Welcome to business & Economics. We start where the subject starts: at the beginning. I am Professor Francisco Rivera, and this is Economics I — Scarcity, Prices, and Why Markets Move — a class in Business & Economics at Exolex University. Here is the whole course, taught unit by unit, in order.
Unit 1 of 6: Scarcity: the first fact.
Unit 2 of 6: Supply and demand: the two curves that run the world.
Unit 3 of 6: Price as a signal, not a verdict.
Unit 4 of 6: Elasticity: how much, when the price moves.
Unit 5 of 6: Money: what it is when everyone agrees.
Unit 6 of 6: Booms, busts, and the stories we tell about them.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: A frost ruins half the orange crop. Trace, in four steps, what happens to the price of orange juice, what juice-makers do next, and what orange growers plant next year. The worked answer: Price rises — the same demand chasing half the fruit. Juice-makers stretch supply: blends, imports, smaller cartons at the old price. Some drinkers switch to apple. And growers, seeing high prices, plant more trees — which fruit in several years, possibly into a glut. That four-beat rhythm — signal, scramble, substitution, investment — is most of economics in one orange.

lesson.teach: Good to see you. Today business & Economics earns its keep. I am Professor Hung Santoso, and this is Money & the Books — Accounting Without Tears — a class in Business & Economics at Exolex University. Here is the whole course, taught unit by unit, in order.
Unit 1 of 6: Double entry: every coin has two stories.
Unit 2 of 6: The three statements: position, performance, cash.
Unit 3 of 6: Assets, liabilities, equity: the grammar of the balance sheet.
Unit 4 of 6: Revenue is not cash, and other expensive confusions.
Unit 5 of 6: Taxes: the appointment every business keeps.
Unit 6 of 6: Reading your own books monthly: the owner's habit.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: Your business is owed $10,000 for work delivered and owes $6,000 to suppliers. Are you 'up $4,000'? Answer in three sentences, carefully. The worked answer: On paper, your position improved by $4,000 — an asset (receivable) exceeds the liability (payable). But you are up zero dollars of cash, and if the $6,000 falls due before the $10,000 arrives, you are in trouble while 'up'. The books tell both truths at once; the skill is reading the second one in time.

lesson.teach: Good to see you. Today business & Economics earns its keep. I am Professor Jessica Baker, and this is Selling — The Honest Craft of the Deal — a class in Business & Economics at Exolex University. Here is the whole course, taught unit by unit, in order.
Unit 1 of 6: Selling as diagnosis: find the problem before the pitch.
Unit 2 of 6: Listening ratios: two ears, one mouth.
Unit 3 of 6: The honest pitch: true claims, plainly made.
Unit 4 of 6: Objections: information, not combat.
Unit 5 of 6: Closing: asking, cleanly, once.
Unit 6 of 6: After the sale: the reputation that sells next time.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: A customer says 'it's too expensive.' Write the two sentences a graduate of this class says next — no discounts, no pressure, and the conversation still alive at the end of them. The worked answer: First: 'Tell me what you were hoping it would do for you — I want to be sure we're pricing the right thing.' Second: 'If it does that, measured in your numbers, what is it worth over a year?' lesson.teach: Good to see you. Today theatre & Film earns its keep. I am Professor Mai Ho, and this is Performance Studies — Performance Everywhere — a class in Theatre & Film at Exolex University. Here is the whole course, taught unit by unit, in order.
Unit 1 of 5: Ritual and performance.
Unit 2 of 5: Performance art.
Unit 3 of 5: Everyday life as performance.
Unit 4 of 5: Digital performance.
Unit 5 of 5: Spectatorship and participation.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: Take Ritual and performance from Performance Studies — Performance Everywhere. Choose one scene — stage or screen — and write five sentences on how it achieves its effect: the choice of shot or staging, the timing, and the one thing you would steal for your own work. The worked answer: This department learns by reverse-engineering effects. Admiration is the entry fee; the homework is theft of technique — naming exactly how the moment was built so your own hands could build one.
